In plain terms, a hacker is someone who thoroughly studies computer systems, devices or networks to understand how they work, modify their behaviour and achieve specific goals. These goals can either be for positive reasons or – as is common in many instances – for negative and even destructive purposes. Therefore, hackers are differentiated by the context that warrants their operations, the permissions given to them and the purpose behind the use of their skills. Tech experts categorise hackers differently. White Hat Hackers (also called ethical hackers) are skilled security specialists who legally probe systems and software to find vulnerabilities and help organisations fix them to prevent malicious individuals from exploiting them. Conversely, cybercriminals are generally known as Black Hat Hackers. These are individuals who gain unauthorised access to systems for malicious purposes. They are known to disrupt networks or computer systems for illegal profit, steal financial data and hold data for ransom using malware – software or code they utilise to intercept or disrupt important information. Last month, the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation, in collaboration with international partners, announced the arrest of nine suspects in Nigeria and the seizure of 53 electronic devices as part of an operation targeting international scam and cybercrime networks. Similarly, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Nigerian Police Force National Cybercrime Centre have carried out multiple stings (including arrests in Lagos and Delta states) targeting online impersonation, cryptocurrency investment scams and romance fraud networks, which often centre around Black Hat Hackers. When hackers gain unauthorised access to your phone, computer or smart home appliance, they can perform a wide range of damaging actions, depending on the type of malware or exploit used. Some of them harvest credit card numbers, bank details, personal IDs, photos and private messages. Using stolen data, cybercriminals can open fraudulent bank or credit card accounts, request new PINs, sell your information on the dark web or, worse, spy on you remotely. “There are spyware or zero-click attacks that can secretly turn on your device’s camera and microphone to record you or snap photos without your knowledge. Hackers can also track your real-time GPS coordinates and movement history. They can log everything you type or take screenshots of your active apps. “Many of these criminals can trick your mobile carrier into transferring your phone number to their SIM card, intercepting your calls, texts and two-factor authentication security codes from banks, and from there, they siphon funds from your account. There are also some who change your social media account passwords or lock your entire device and, in some cases, demand payment to restore access,” a cybersecurity expert, David Odes, explained. Odes further stated that when these hackers gain access to devices, their activities can result in rapid battery drain, severe overheating, high data spikes and sluggish performance. How to protect your device from hackers: Reporters face rare phone restrictions on Air Force One Why Digital Security Matters to Online Casino Players Huawei warns of AI-driven cyber risks Be wary of suspicious messages Posing as bankers, co-workers or tech brands, hackers can trick people into revealing their passwords, debit card numbers or personal identification details and use this information to install malware on their devices. This method is known as phishing. “If you receive an unsolicited email or SMS, or a phone call from a bank asking you to send them a code, or you get a message on a messaging platform asking you to click on a link to claim some benefits, be very careful. You may be clicking on suspicious links or a malware file, which can cause your account to be compromised,” Odes advised. Check your device A regular audit of apps and devices will enable users to scrutinise third-party app permissions or notice if their phones begin to frequently overheat or become slow in operation. “This can also happen to your laptop. If you notice that the camera lens is suddenly turned on without your permission, contact your tech support at work. Ensure you also remove any old accounts, unused apps or unfamiliar linked devices from your security dashboard,” a tech consultant, Solomon Nwadike, advised. Stop reusing passwords Nwadike advised that passwords for devices, bank apps, social media accounts and platforms used for online transactions should be varied and unique. “You can use the password manager to generate and store long, unique passwords for every account. Avoid repeating passwords so a breach on one site doesn’t affect the others,” he said. Enable multi-factor authentication Adding a second verification step, which could include a code through an authenticator app or a security key, can help protect your device. “This can safeguard your email, bank and social media accounts. This type of authentication will help block most unauthorised access even if your password leaks to hackers,” Odes said. Update regularly Consistently updating software on mobile apps, smart TVs and other devices will prevent them from becoming compromised and help safeguard them from hackers. “When you regularly update software on your device, it will look for newly discovered security flaws and fix them before hackers can exploit them,” Nwadike advised.
